# Western hemlock

## Summary info for Hw

### Col - Tree image {width="20%"}


```{r}

#| fig-cap: "Western hemlock (*Tsuga heterophylla*) <br> Image credit: NRCan"

### Col - Welcome text {width="80%"}

**Western hemlock (abbreviated Hw) is one of the most common conifer species in the Coast and Interior Cordillera regions of British Columbia and is an important timber species for pulp and lumber products. The CCISS model predicts a decline or loss of suitability in the warmest and/or driest parts of its historical range. Increases and expansion of Hw environmental suitability are predicted upslope throughout the Coastal, Columbia and Rocky Mountain ranges, as well as into newly suitable areas of the Sub-Boreal Interior.** <br>

While the CCISS tool offers valuable insights into broad-scale trends, summarized here by species, suitability projections must be interpreted with caution. Many areas of projected change are also areas with high uncertainty in climate predictions. Furthermore, factors such as soil texture, drainage, land-use history, forest health pressures, and biotic interactions (e.g., competition or browsing) can strongly influence actual outcomes on the ground. These nuances emphasize the importance of pairing climate tools with on-the-ground knowledge and site-specific judgement when planning future western hemlock management.

# Reference period

## Summary text

**Species geographic and climatic range**

Western hemlock (Hw) occurs in cool temperate and cool mesothermal climates of the Pacific coast and Interior Cordilleran regions of Western North America. It is found throughout the Coast Mountains from northern BC and the Alaska panhandle to northern California, and throughout the interior wetbelt in the Columbia and Rocky Mountains in BC and northern Washington, Idaho, and Montana [@nrcan_western_hemlock; @arno2020northwest].

Hw is found in both submontane and montane habitats (up to subalpine) on a wide range of soil moisture and nutrient regimes [@klinka_distribution_2000; @Packee1990]. It prefers fresh to very moist soil, but can tolerate wetter conditions by growing on mounds or decomposing stumps. It thrives on very poor to medium soil nutrient regimes, and where acidic coniferous decaying wood is plentiful. Mycorrhizal associations are common with Hw seedlings establishing in both soil and decaying wood [@kropp_fungi_1982]. It is very shade-tolerant and shade cover is required for robust seedling establishment [@hetherington_western_hemlock_establishment]. Because of this shade tolerance, it tends to be the dominant tree in dense forests that have not seen disturbance for long time periods [@arno2020northwest]. Hw is adapted to the long growing season characteristic of humid coastal climates and low elevation regions of the interior wetbelt, and its shallow roots do not tolerate frozen ground unless it is covered with insulating snow before freezing [@klinka_distribution_2000].

**Species environmental suitability during the reference period (1961--1990)**

In the maps below, each colour represents the species environmental suitability during the historical reference period\* of 1961--90 as determined by expert ratings. Green represents a high suitability (E1 rating), blue represents moderate suitability (E2), yellow represents low suitability (E3), and white indicates areas that are unsuitable for the species. See [CCISS Documentation tab \> Methods \> Environmental Suitability Ratings](https://bcgov-ffec.ca/cciss-docs/Methods.html#environmental-suitability-ratings) for more detailed definitions and information on the expert rating process.

\*Notes on terminology: 1) The historical reference period is sometimes referred to as the "baseline" or simply "historical" or "reference" period. 2) Edatope refers to the combination of relative soil nutrient regime and soil moisture  regime at a given site which align with distinct site series in a given biogeoclimatic unit. Here we provide three of the possible edatopes as examples: the B2 edatope representing nutrient-poor and relatively dry (subxeric) sites; the C4 edatope representing nutrient-medium and moisture-average (mesic) sites; and the D6 edatope representing nutrient-rich and relatively moist (hygric) sites.

Suitability is low (E3) along the western shore of Haida Gwaii where scrub forest and blanket bogs dominate, as well as the colder MH, ICH, ESSF, and SBS subzones on the north and eastern edges of the Coast Mountains and high elevation and/or drier subzones throughout the Coast region. ```{r}

In contrast, large areas of the hypermaritime coastal range drop to moderate (E2) or low (E3) suitability, as well as the wetter and/or colder subzones throughout Hw's range (e.g., ICHmw1 near Golden, ICHmc2 in the Skeena River drainage, and MHmm1 at higher elevation on the coast). In some otherwise unsuitable zones, like the CDFmm along the Strait of Georgia, higher moisture in D6 edatopic pockets allow for low (E3) suitability. Remaining areas (in white) are unsuitable for Hw under historic climates on rich/hygric sites.

fig("Historic_Suit_Map.Hw.D6.png")
```

### BGC text

**Distribution of Hw across BGC zones**

The pie chart to the right depicts the distribution of the total environmentally suitable area of Hw in BC by biogeoclimatic (BGC) zone, based on the climate of the historical reference period (1961--1990).

The majority of Hw's range occurs in the Coastal Western Hemlock (CWH) zone along the coast, where it is the characteristic tree species [@ecosystems_bc_1991; @centre_for_forest_conservation_genetics_cataloguing_nodate]. Hw is the most common tree species and together with western redcedar (Cw) is generally frequent throughout the zone. Hw and Cw co-occur alongside a variety of other species depending on the climate (e.g. Douglas-fir in the drier and warmer subzones; Amabilis fir in the wetter and cooler subzones; yellow-cedar in the wetter subzones) and/or local conditions (e.g. shore pine on very dry or wet sites, alders on disturbed sites, cottonwood on floodplains) [@centre_for_forest_conservation_genetics_cataloguing_nodate].

It is also a characteristic species of the Interior Cedar-Hemlock (ICH) zone in the lower and middle elevations of the Skeena and Nass River drainages, the lower slopes of the Columbia Mountains, and west of the continental divide along the Rocky Mountains. The ICH has high tree species diversity. Hw is the most common tree species, followed by Cw, which co-occur alongside many other tree species. Hw and Cw dominate old-growth stands in most subzones of both the CWH and ICH [@centre_for_forest_conservation_genetics_cataloguing_nodate].

In the Coast Mountains, Hw also occurs in the subalpine Mountain Hemlock (MH) zone, where it co-occurs with the more common mountain hemlock (Hm), particularly in the ecotone along the upper edge of the CWH [@ecosystems_bc_1991]. Similarly, in the interior subalpine, Hw occurs in the ecotone between the ICH and the Engelmann Spruce -- Subalpine Fir (ESSF) zone.

To a much lesser extent, Hw can also be found in the Montane Spruce (MS) and Sub-Boreal Spruce (SBS) zones at the colder edge of its tolerance, and the Interior Douglas-fir (IDF), and Coastal Douglas-fir (CDF) zones at the drier end of its tolerance, though its environmental suitability in these zones is mostly moderate to low (E2-E3).

([Government of British Columbia 2025](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/forestry/managing-our-forest-resources/silviculture/stocking-standards/tree-species-compendium-index/western-hemlock)).

# CCISS projections

## Overall summary

**Future projected environmental suitability for western hemlock**

On this page, you will find a visual and interpretive synthesis of the environmental suitability projections calculated using the Climate Change Informed Species Selection [CCISS](https://bcgov-ffec.ca/cciss-docs/) tool, including:

1.  Proportion of the historic range that the species is predicted to remain environmentally suitable (i.e. persist) or become newly suitable (i.e. expand) by site type (edatope).

2.  Predicted mean changes in environmental suitability across its geographic range in BC, by future time period and site type (edatope).

3.  Predicted shifts in total suitable area over time across the province and by biogeoclimatic (BGC) zone.

## Row - Bubble plot {height="700px"}

### L Column - Plot description {width="40%"}

::: card
Western hemlock (Hw) is projected to persist within 55-70% of its historically suitable range, and its suitable range is projected to expand into an additional area about 30-70% the size of its historical area. When this expansion is combined with the loss of historically suitable area, the overall suitable area is projected to stay about the same over time (as shown by the blue dot in the figure remaining close to the grey dashed line - see figure legend). This trend varies somewhat by site type. In zonal (C4) and rich/hygric (D6) sites, the total area suitable for Hw is projected to expand slightly over time as warming climate conditions shift its suitable habitat upslope and into more northern latitudes, whereas total suitable area in poor/subxeric (B2) sites is projected to decrease over time, primarily due to the increasing drought stress projected for future time periods. <br>

*Notes on interpretation of persistence and expansion*

Persistence (x-axis) and expansion (y-axis) are subtly different in how they relate to the historical range of the species. Persistence describes the change in environmental suitability within the species historical range. Expansion describes the change in environmental suitability outside of the species historical range. Calculated as follows:

$$\text{Persistence (\%)} =
\frac{\text{future suitable area within historical range of suitability}}
{\text{historically suitable area}}
\times 100$$

$$\text{Expansion (\%)} =
\frac{\text{future suitable area outside historical range of suitability}}
{\text{historically suitable area}}
\times 100$$
:::

## Row {.spacer-row}

**Suitability changes**

## Row - Maps {height="800px"}

### L col {width="35%"}

::: card
The CCISS model generally predicts that environmental suitability for Hw will increase upslope of its historical range, and decrease at lower elevations within its current range where the climate is projected to become too hot and/or dry to support it. Particularly, suitability declines and losses are projected to be highest in the drier subzones of the low-elevation Coastal Western Hemlock (CWH) and Interior Cedar-Hemlock (ICH) zones, including the CWHdm2, CWHxs, and ICHdw1. However, many other parts of Hw's coastal range that were historically highly suitable are projected to remain suitable due to the stabilizing influence of the ocean on coastal climates. For example, in the very wet coastal forest subzones of the CWH, Hw suitability is projected to be maintained into the 2081-2100 period in many places (e.g., CHWvm3), or experience decreases in moisture (e.g., the climate of CWHvh2 is projected to become more CWHvm3-like along parts of the northern coast near Bella Bella) that are still well within the suitability range for Hw.

As climate change increases regional temperatures over the next 80 years, Hw's suitability is projected to increase and expand in higher elevation zones, such as the Mountain Hemlock (MH), Engelmann Spruce -- Subalpine Fir (ESSF), and even current alpine zones (e.g., the Coastal Mountain-heather Alpine (CMA) and Interior Mountain-heather Alpine (IMA)) as they are projected to become more climatically similar to CWH and MH in the Coast Mountains, and ICH-like in the Columbia Mountains.

The CCISS model also predicts expansion of suitable habitat for Hw over the course of the century, particularly into medium/mesic (C4) sites of the Sub-Boreal Spruce (SBS) zone in the Interior Plateau. Warming is projected in this region, causing it to become more ICH-like over this time period, which will make it suitable for both western redcedar and Hw. Expansion of Hw suitability into medium/mesic (C4) and rich/hygric (D6) sites is also predicted for the Montane Spruce (MS) zone, on the Thompson Plateau, Fraser Plateau and the Shuswap Highland (e.g., MSdm variants), as they are projected to become warmer and wetter with climate change.

There is lower confidence in the expansion of Hw suitability into the Coastal Douglas-fir (CDF) zone. The future climate in this area is projected to be more similar to that of CWHxm_WA (very dry warm CWH from Washington), a warmer but wetter unit from further south, surrounding Puget Sound. Note that there is a higher degree of climate novelty in the CCISS projections in this area of the province, meaning the projected future climate is not well captured by the closest climate analog (in this case the CWHxm_WA) (see documentation about [novel climates](https://bcgov-ffec.ca/cciss-docs/Methods.html#novel-climate-detection)). There is higher uncertainty around results in areas of climatic novelty; use caution when interpreting.

:::

### Col - description {width="40%"}

Hw's total suitable area is projected to expand over the 21st century, due to an overall fairly stable suitable area in its core range, in the Coastal Western Hemlock (CWH) and Interior Cedar-Hemlock (ICH) zones (despite losses of suitability in drought-prone subzones, as described above), as well as an increase in suitable area particularly in the Engelmann Spruce-–Subalpine Fir (ESSF) and Sub-Boreal Spruce (SBS) zones.

Wet subzone/variants in the lower elevation portions of the ESSF zone are projected to undergo shifts toward more Interior Cedar–Hemlock (ICH)-like climates, which means that the increased suitable area projected for Hw in this higher-elevation zone may lead to up-slope movement of the species. Many mapped units within the SBS zone, especially wetter subzone variants, are also projected to become warmer and wetter over time, shifting towards more ICH-like climates in the future, driving an increase in suitability for Hw. To a much smaller extent in area, this is also true of the Sub-Boreal Pine--Spruce (SBPS) zone.

The Mountain Hemlock (MH) zone is above the CWH zone in elevation throughout the Coast Mountains and historically supported populations of Hw at lower elevations of the zone, but with only low (E3) to moderate (E2) suitability. While this zone does not see a large expansion of suitable area projected, Hw is projected to increase in suitability (up to high (E1) suitability) in many areas by 2100. A similar trend is projected for the Montane Spruce (MS) zone, where Hw had historically low to moderate suitability; as climate change warms this higher-elevation zone, its Hw suitability is projected to increase.

As described above, small areas of the CDF and IDF are projected to potentially become suitable (low (E3) to moderate (E2)) for Hw due to projected increases in precipitation. Although note that the CDF covers an area of high climate novelty, meaning the projected future climate is not well captured by the closest climate analog (see documentation about [novel climates](https://bcgov-ffec.ca/cciss-docs/Methods.html#novel-climate-detection)). There is higher uncertainty around results in areas of climatic novelty, use caution when interpreting.

Small alpine areas of the CMA, BAFA, and IMA are also projected to become suitable as they warm to become more similar to the BGC zones below them in elevation. Additionally, the more northern-latitude Spruce--Willow--Birch (SWB) and Boreal White and Black Spruce (BWBS) zones are projected to become suitable in small areas as they experience warming climates but there is more model uncertainty here in whether that warming will lead to them being climatically similar to Hw-suitable zones. For example, a portion of the future projections for the SWBmk subzone suggest that it will become ICH-like with higher temperatures and precipitation, but a variety of other possibilities include becoming more climatically similar to the MS, SBS, and BWBS zones, which would not be suitable for Hw.

# Forest health

## Biotic factors text

**Biotic factors**

*Defoliating insects*

Western hemlock (Hw) is host to a variety of defoliators, including the western hemlock looper (*Lambdina fiscellaria lugubrosa*), green-striped forest looper (*Melanolophia imitata*), western blackheaded budworm (*Acleris gloverana*), conifer sawflies (*Neodiprion* spp.), and occasionally the western false hemlock looper (*Nepytia freemani*) [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. Hw is intolerant of defoliation and may experience growth loss or mortality after a single year of heavy attack. Risk generally increases with repeated years of defoliation, and damage may be compounded when multiple defoliator species attack different age classes of foliage simultaneously. Mortality can continue for years following the collapse of an infestation, and damage may pre-dispose Hw to secondary attacks by other insects or fungi [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. Impacts might be more severe in young, spaced stands less than 25 years old [@nealis2010impact].

The western hemlock looper's wasteful feeding habit makes it particularly damaging for Hw, and occurs most commonly in valley bottoms [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. Similarly, the green-striped forest looper prefers Hw as a host species and can cause high mortality in the understory along the coast and interior wet belt [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc].

*Other insects*

Bark and root-collar beetles are generally secondary pests of Hw, primarily attacking trees that are already stressed, dying, or recently killed. Species including Hylurgops beetles (*Hylurgops rugipennis*), silver fir beetles (*Pseudohylesinus grandis*), and fir root bark beetles (*Pseudohylesinus granulatus*) contribute to decline and wood degradation but are typically not important mortality agents in vigorous stands [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. The hylurgops beetle in particular is a secondary pest that attacks 15+ year old mature trees, usually if already stressed. Otherwise, they attack stumps and dead or dying wood material.

Western hemlock seedlings may be damaged or killed by conifer seedling weevils (*Steremnius carinatus*), particularly on cool, moist, rich sites. Populations build up in debris-covered previously-logged sites, but attack most strongly in sites where ground cover has been cleared prior to replanting [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc].

Hw is also host to the hemlock woolly adelgid (*Adelges tsugae*), and -- unlike populations of Eastern hemlock that have been devastated by infestations after the adelgid was accidentally introduced -- is tolerant to its presence and feeding. Hw's tolerance is also accentuated by the presence of native parasitoids which keep adelgid populations low [@kohler2008parasitoids]. Thus, mortality of Hw from the hemlock woolly adelgid alone is usually low [@CFIA_HemlockWoollyAdelgid].

*Fungal pathogens and decomposers*

Root rot can cause substantial growth loss, structural weakening, and mortality in Hw [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. Root diseases such as tomentosus (*Onnia tomentosa*) and annosus (*Heterobasidion occidentale*) root rot and Armillaria root disease (*Armillaria ostoyae*) contribute to mortality, especially in younger stands or where infection centers become established. Rhizina root disease (*Rhizina undulata*) occurs within the first two years following a fire.

Several pathogens affect shoots, branches, and young trees [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. Sirococcus tip blight (*Sirococcus conigenus*) damages current-year shoots in dense, moist stands, while Phomopsis canker (*Diaporthe lokoyae*) may girdle small trees and cause branch or top dieback in larger individuals.

Numerous heart-rot and butt-rot fungi affect Hw, including brown crumbly rot (*Fomitopsis pinicola*), brown trunk rot (*Fomitopsis officinalis*), red ring rot (*Fomitopsis officinalis*), Indian paint fungus (*Echinodontium tinctorium*), and Schweinitzii butt rot (*Phaeolus schweinitzii*) [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. These fungi are most common on dead material as important decomposers in the ecosystem, but can enter living trees through wounds, bored holes, branch stubs, or damage from snow and can substantially reduce wood quality and structural integrity long before external fruiting bodies (typically conks) become visible on the trunk surface.

Hemlock dwarf mistletoe (*Arceuthobium tsugense*) is a common and serious threat to Hw stands in the coastal populations but not interior. In highly productive Hw sites, trees can outgrow the mistletoe, but it can spread very easily and can infect large portions of a hemlock stand within several decades [@burleigh2014_forest_damage_bc]. It reduces growth, water use efficiency, photosynthetic capacity, and total foliage and can severely deform woody tissue [@calkins2021transformation; @marias2014impacts; @meinzer2004integrated].

For more information see the [Forest Guide to Tree Health](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/farming-natural-resources-and-industry/forestry/forest-health/forest-health-docs/field_guide_to_forest_damage_in_bc_web.pdf) and [Natural Resources Canada](https://tidcf.nrcan.gc.ca/en/trees/factsheet/119). To view forest health risk across BGC subzone by tree species and biotic factor see the "Forest Health" tab of the [By-BEC Portal](https://thebeczone.ca/shiny/bybecmap/).

## Abiotic factors

**Abiotic factors**

Western hemlock is vulnerable to high winds, freezing, drought, and fire. Its shallow roots and thin bark make Hw particularly vulnerable to freezing and fire [@arno2020northwest]. These shallow roots also give it low resistance to windthrow [@klinka_distribution_2000]. Hw's distribution is limited to areas that either do not freeze or that receive snow prior to the ground freezing, and while it might tolerate frost, its vigor is reduced by frost damage, resulting in many quickly shed leaves [@klinka_distribution_2000]. It tolerates drought better than Pacific silver fir, one of its more common montane associates [@arno2020northwest], but due to its high water requirements, it requires shade protection from both drought and heat to be able to survive [@klinka_distribution_2000].

## Climate change-forest health interactions

**Potential effects of climate change**

In general, the increasing temperatures associated with climate change will likely be more beneficial for short-lived and rapidly responsive pest and pathogen species than for their longer-lived hosts [@Woods2010; @Coakley1999]. They will also likely be able to track their favorable climates more quickly than their hosts, since warming tends to accelerate insect and fungal development and favor range expansion (in comparison to long-lived tree species, which tend to lag in their ability to track their suitable environments) [@Ayres2000].

Drought stress is a known starting point for disease and pest attack [@Woods2010]. With Hw's sensitivity to drought, it will likely be impacted by pests more strongly in the future, particularly in the parts of its historical range that are projected to become unfavorably warm and dry (e.g., many drier subzones of the CWH and ICH) over the next several decades. For example, outbreaks of the western hemlock looper have been associated with soil moisture deficits [@McCloskey2009]. Thus, the true suitability of these zones might be lower than what is projected by climate change alone.

As extreme weather patterns and the severity of storms increase from climate change, windthrow of conifers (particularly Hw, due to their shallow root systems) will likely become more common. Accumulating downed trees can harbor pest populations, such as the conifer seedling weevil and multiple bark beetle species [@Woods2010], leading to potentially more severe and sustained attacks to nearby and otherwise healthy stands.

While insects outbreaks are heavily controlled by temperature, pathogens are more affected by precipitation patterns, but the ability of some fungi to overwinter might also improve with warming [@Woods2010]. Increased precipitation during the growing season will be particularly beneficial for stem rust fungi, whereas their prevalence might decrease in their current ranges where precipitation is projected to decrease [@Woods2010]. In contrast, root diseases will likely increase in prevalence throughout much of BC's Interior, since they tend to take advantage of drought-stressed trees [@Woods2010]. Similarly, the range of hemlock dwarf mistletoe may expand inland and upslope as temperatures rise and winter snowfall decreases [@Woods2010].
